items.summary: The same branch, busier: PHONE's calls (512 kb/s, EF), VIDEO's conference room (3 Mb/s, marked AF41 by the endpoint), PC1's application (2 Mb/s of HTTPS) and web browsing (2 Mb/s of HTTP), and BACKUP's FTP (20 Mb/s), over a 10 Mb/s WAN. The standard: the voice and video LAN (Gi0/0) is trusted; the data LAN (Gi0/2) is re-marked by an input policy EDGE-IN (HTTPS af21, FTP cs1, everything else default). WAN-OUT on Gi0/1: VOICE (ef) priority percent 10; VIDEO (af41) bandwidth percent 35; CRITICAL (af21) bandwidth percent 25; SCAVENGER (cs1) bandwidth percent 5; class-default fair-queue. Calls, video, the application and the web lose nothing; the backup takes what's left.

items.title: QoS: find the fault
items.summary: R1 marks the data LAN at the edge (EDGE-IN on Gi0/2) and queues the 10 Mb/s WAN by DSCP (WAN-OUT on Gi0/1), and it worked: calls clean, the application whole, the backup scavenging. Then someone changed a class map, a policy or an interface, or a PC started marking its own traffic. The symptom is a flow; Get-TrafficFlow's trainer note and show policy-map interface say where it loses and which class it landed in.

items.title: Expand: a 100 Mb/s handoff with a 10 Mb/s contract
items.summary: The leased line is replaced by a provider's Ethernet service: a 100 Mb/s port on PE, but the contract is 10 Mb/s, and PE polices what R1 sends to that rate (CONTRACT-10M). R1's WAN-OUT is still applied, and now does nothing: at 100 Mb/s R1's link is never congested, so its queues never fill, and the provider's policer drops the excess from every flow alike, calls included. Shape to the contract on R1, with WAN-OUT inside the shaper (hierarchical QoS), so R1 decides what waits and the policer has nothing to drop.

items.title: Know it: reading a QoS configuration
items.group: QoS architecture: DiffServ, IntServ and MPLS

items.title: Read: debugs, and how to use them without hurting anyone
Learn: let the router say what's wrong
items.summary: R1 and R2 should be OSPF neighbors over the WAN link, and aren't: show ip ospf neighbor on R1 is empty and PC-A can't reach the server NMS (10.1.20.50). Nothing in the configuration looks wrong at a glance. Turn on the debug that reads hellos, read what R2 is sending, fix it, then watch a ping cross R1 with debug ip packet aimed by an access list.

items.title: Build it: a debug aimed at one conversation
items.summary: The help desk says ADMIN (10.1.20.10) sometimes can't reach PC-A (10.1.10.10) and wants R1 watched for a while. R1 carries everyone's traffic, so a bare debug ip packet is out of the question. Build a debug that prints only that conversation, in detail, limited to the WAN interface, plus the ICMP debug, and leave it running for the check.

items.title: Debugs: find the fault
items.summary: Something between R1 and R2, or on R1's DHCP, broke overnight: PC-A can't reach NMS (10.1.20.50), or has no address at all. show commands show absence; the debugs show cause. Find it from R1 with debug ip ospf hello, debug ip ospf adj and debug ip dhcp server events, fix it, and turn the debugs off again.

items.title: Expand: debugs over an SSH session
items.summary: You manage R1 from ADMIN (10.1.20.10) over SSH, not from its console. Turn on debug ip icmp there and make the output reach your session: terminal monitor asks for it, and logging monitor on R1 decides what a remote session may see. Someone set it to warnings.

items.title: Read: IP SLA for performance, not just reachability
items.group: IP SLA: jitter, delay and responders

items.title: Learn: measure a path, not just reach it
items.summary: HQ already runs two udp-jitter operations toward BR: operation 10 over the MPLS circuit, 20 over the satellite link, both scored for voice. Both say No connection: a UDP probe needs someone to answer at the far end. Turn BR into an IP SLA responder, read what each path really does to voice, then put a threshold on the satellite path and watch a state object and a reachability object disagree about it.
items.group: IP SLA: jitter, delay and responders

items.title: Build it: probes for voice, SSH and the server
items.summary: The voice team wants to know how each WAN path treats calls, the operations team wants to know that BR's SSH answers and that the server is up. On HQ, build four operations: udp-jitter to 10.1.1.1 from g0/1 and to 10.1.1.2 from g0/0, both on port 16384 with codec g711ulaw; tcp-connect to 10.1.1.1 port 22 from g0/1; icmp-echo to 10.2.20.50 from g0/1 every 30 seconds. Schedule them all, give operation 10 a 100 ms threshold, and follow it with track 10 (state). BR must answer the UDP probes.
items.group: IP SLA: jitter, delay and responders

items.title: IP SLA: find the fault
items.summary: The four probes on HQ ran fine for weeks. This morning one of them reports a failure, or a number that can't be right. Read show ip sla statistics and show track, find what changed on HQ or BR, and fix it. The probes themselves must keep measuring what they were built to measure.
items.group: IP SLA: jitter, delay and responders

items.title: Expand: a permanent responder port, no control messages
items.summary: Security won't allow the responder's control protocol (UDP 1967) on BR any more: ip sla responder is gone, and operations 10 and 20 report No connection. Keep the probes working without it: give BR permanent responder ports for 16384 on both loopbacks, tell the operations not to send control messages, and add a udp-echo operation 50 to 10.1.1.1 port 5000 the same way.
items.group: IP SLA: jitter, delay and responders

items.title: Read: SPAN, RSPAN and ERSPAN, or how to see someone else's packets
Learn: copy a port to the analyzer, then to the next switch
items.summary: Two PCs, two switches, a router and a server. SNIFFER is cabled to SW1's Gi0/4 and runs a capture, yet it sees nothing but its own traffic: a switch delivers frames only where they belong. Make SW1 copy PC-A's port to the analyzer with a SPAN session, read the copies on SNIFFER, then carry copies of PC-B's port across the trunk to NOC on SW2 with RSPAN.

items.title: Build it: an analyzer on PC-A's port, the NOC on the uplink
items.summary: Security wants everything PC-A sends copied to SNIFFER on SW1 Gi0/4, VLAN tags intact, and nothing PC-A receives. The NOC wants both directions of the uplink to the router (SW1 Gi0/5) on NOC, which hangs off SW2's Gi0/3. Build a local SPAN session for the first (session 1), an RSPAN session in VLAN 999 for the second (session 2 on SW1, session 1 on SW2), start captures on both analyzers and prove the copies arrive.

items.title: SPAN: find the fault
items.summary: Both mirrors worked last week: SW1's session 1 copies PC-A's port (both ways) to SNIFFER, and the uplink Gi0/5 reaches NOC over RSPAN VLAN 999. This morning one analyzer shows the wrong traffic, half of it, or nothing. The captures are still running on both PCs. Find what changed on SW1 or SW2, fix it, make traffic, and prove the copies are back.

items.title: Expand: ERSPAN from the router to the NOC
items.summary: NOC wants to see the server's side of the router, Gi0/1, where no switch and no RSPAN VLAN can reach: the port is on R1. ERSPAN wraps the copies in GRE and routes them to an IP address. Build an ERSPAN source session on R1 that mirrors Gi0/1 both ways to NOC (10.1.10.201) with ERSPAN ID 10 and origin 10.1.10.1, and read the copies on NOC.

items.title: Read: RESTCONF and NETCONF, the router as an API
Learn: the same router through RESTCONF and NETCONF
items.summary: R1 (10.1.1.1) is managed over SSH and its HTTPS web UI, logins against the local user admin (N3tdrill-API). Turn on its two programmable interfaces and use them from DEV, a Linux PC: RESTCONF with curl (JSON over HTTPS: discover the root, read the interfaces, change a description), NETCONF with netconf-console (XML over SSH on port 830: the hello's capabilities, then get-config). ADMIN, a Windows PC, does the same with Invoke-RestMethod.

items.title: Build it: RESTCONF and NETCONF, locked down like the web UI
items.summary: The automation team wants R1 reachable over RESTCONF and NETCONF from the management LAN (10.1.1.0/24) and nowhere else: HTTPS only, logins against the local privilege-15 user admin, a standard access list API-HOSTS as the web server's access class, restconf and netconf-yang on. Prove it from DEV, and set Gi0/1's description to Uplink to R2 through the API rather than the CLI.

items.title: RESTCONF and NETCONF: find the fault
items.summary: R1's APIs worked: the automation scripts read and wrote it from DEV over RESTCONF and NETCONF. This morning they fail: a 404, a 401, a refused connection, or no answer at all. Each failure comes from a different layer (the API switch, the HTTPS server, the login method, the user, the access list, the SSH key); the status code says which.

items.title: Expand: create and delete with RESTCONF
items.summary: Reading is half of it. Give R1 a new loopback entirely through the API: PUT https://10.1.1.1/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=Loopback100 with a body naming the interface, its type (iana-if-type:softwareLoopback), enabled, and an ietf-ip:ipv4 address of 172.16.100.1/32. Then remove the old Loopback99 (172.16.99.1) with DELETE. Watch the status codes: 201 Created, 204 No Content, and what a second PUT or a DELETE of something that doesn't exist says.

items.title: Read: EEM, a router that reacts to its own events
Learn: a router that fixes its own default route
items.summary: R1 is a partner site's branch router: no routing protocol toward the data center, just a static default through R2 (10.0.12.2). The link to R3 (10.0.13.2) is a metered backup, to be used only after a real failure and never silently. Write an EEM applet that watches for Gi0/1 going down, adds a default route through R3 and tells the NOC with a syslog message; then test it with shutdown and no shutdown.

items.title: Build it: failover, failback and a backup on every save
items.summary: The branch standard asks R1 for three applets. WAN-DOWN: on the Gi0/1 down message, add ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.0.13.2 and log a critical message. WAN-UP: on "Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to up", remove that route and log a notification (anchor the pattern on the line-protocol message: a link coming up logs a %LINK and a %LINEPROTO message, and a pattern both contain runs the applet twice, the second time against a route that is already gone). SAVE-BACKUP: whenever someone types write memory, copy the running configuration to the TFTP server on PC-A (10.1.1.10) as R1-backup.cfg and log that it was done, quoting the command through $_cli_msg.

items.title: EEM applets: find the fault
items.summary: R1's three applets worked: the failover drill last month switched the default route to R3 within a second and the NOC got its message. Someone has since edited them, and the latest drill failed quietly: the link went down, nothing happened, no message. An applet that does nothing leaves few traces: compare the pattern with the message the router really logs, the order the actions run in, the mode each command needs, and whether the router logs at all.

items.title: Expand: data collection on demand with event none
items.summary: Not every applet waits for something to happen. The NOC wants one command that gathers R1's interface table, routing table and applet history in one go: an applet with event none, run by hand with event manager run COLLECT, whose cli actions capture each show command's output in $_cli_result and whose puts actions print it. The variables are the point: $_cli_result holds the last cli command's output, $_syslog_msg the message that triggered a syslog applet, $_cli_msg the command that triggered a cli applet.

items.title: Know it: agent-based and agentless orchestration tools
Read: VXLAN, a VLAN across a routed fabric
Learn: VXLAN on a working fabric
items.summary: Three leaves, each in its own rack, with a server in VLAN 10 and the same subnet everywhere (10.10.10.0/24). Between the racks everything is routed, yet the servers ping each other as if on one switch: VLAN 10 rides in VNI 10010 over the fabric. See how, then add a server to the segment.

items.title: Build it: one VLAN across three racks (VXLAN)
items.summary: The fabric is routed: OSPF runs between the spines and the leaves, and each leaf has a loopback (10.255.0.11, .12, .13). Each rack has a server in VLAN 10, all in 10.10.10.0/24, but a VLAN ends at the leaf's routed uplinks, so they can't reach each other. Carry VLAN 10 between the leaves in VNI 10010.

items.title: VXLAN: find the fault
items.summary: Three leaves carry VLAN 10 in VNI 10010 between the racks, each with a flood list of the other two leaves' loopbacks (10.255.0.11, .12, .13), over an OSPF underlay. Some servers can't reach each other, maybe in one direction only. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: a second segment, on two racks only
items.summary: The web team needs its own segment: VLAN 20 (WEB, 10.20.20.0/24) in VNI 10020, for WEB1 on LEAF1 Gi0/2 and WEB3 on LEAF3 Gi0/2. LEAF2 has no web servers, so it shouldn't receive their broadcasts: its flood lists stay as they are.

items.title: Read: BGP EVPN, the control plane for VXLAN
Learn: BGP EVPN on a working fabric
items.summary: The three-rack VXLAN fabric again, but no flood list is typed anywhere: the leaves peer over iBGP between their loopbacks and learn each other through BGP EVPN. See what they exchange, then carry a second VLAN and watch its flood lists build themselves.

items.title: Build it: replace the static flood lists with BGP EVPN
items.summary: The fabric from the VXLAN topic works, with a flood list typed on every leaf. Every new leaf would mean editing every list, so move the fabric to BGP EVPN: the leaves peer over iBGP (AS 65000) between their loopbacks, and each learns the others' VTEPs from BGP.

items.title: BGP EVPN: find the fault
items.summary: Three leaves carry VLAN 10 in VNI 10010, and learn each other through BGP EVPN: iBGP (AS 65000) between their loopbacks (10.255.0.11, .12, .13), every neighbor activated under address-family l2vpn evpn with extended communities, nve1 with host-reachability protocol bgp. OSPF is the underlay. Some servers can't reach each other, maybe in one direction only. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: a fourth leaf joins
items.summary: LEAF4 is racked, cabled to both spines and in the underlay (OSPF, loopback 10.255.0.14), with SRV4 in VLAN 10. Bring it into the EVPN fabric. Nobody edits a flood list: the other leaves only need LEAF4 as a BGP neighbor. (Large fabrics avoid even that with route reflectors on the spines; NetDrill doesn't model them.)

items.title: Read: anycast gateways, routing between VNIs
Learn: an anycast gateway on a working fabric
items.summary: The EVPN fabric carries two segments, VLAN 10 (servers, 10.10.10.0/24) and VLAN 20 (web, 10.20.20.0/24), and every leaf is the gateway for both: the same address and MAC on each. See who routes what, then add a web server to a rack that has none.

items.title: Build it: an anycast gateway on every leaf
items.summary: The EVPN fabric carries VLAN 10 (servers) on every leaf, and VLAN 20 (web) on LEAF1 and LEAF3, where the web servers are. Servers reach servers and web servers reach web servers, but not each other: there is no gateway yet. Make every leaf the gateway for both VLANs, with the same address and MAC everywhere.

items.title: Anycast gateway: find the fault
items.summary: Every leaf is the gateway for VLAN 10 (10.10.10.1) and VLAN 20 (10.20.20.1), with MAC 0000.2222.3333 everywhere, and carries both VNIs (10010, 10020) over BGP EVPN. Servers are in VLAN 10 on every leaf, web servers in VLAN 20 on LEAF1 and LEAF3. Something is off: traffic fails, or takes the long way. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: a third segment, with its gateway on every leaf
items.summary: An application tier joins: VLAN 30 (APP, 10.30.30.0/24, VNI 10030), with APP2 cabled to LEAF2 Gi0/2 (10.30.30.12, gateway 10.30.30.1). Every rack's servers must reach it, so every leaf needs the segment and its gateway, including the leaves with no APP server.

items.title: Read: troubleshooting a VXLAN EVPN fabric
Learn: MTU and route targets on a working fabric
items.summary: The BGP EVPN fabric, run the way production fabrics are: the fabric links carry jumbo frames, so VXLAN's extra 50 bytes always fit, and VLAN 10's route targets are set by hand in an EVPN instance. See both at work, then fix a link that came back from a repair at the default MTU.

items.title: Build it: jumbo frames and route targets set by hand
items.summary: The EVPN fabric works for small packets, but every fabric link runs the default MTU, 1500: a full-size server packet plus VXLAN's 50 bytes doesn't fit, so it's dropped. Route targets are automatic (AS:VNI). Give the fabric jumbo frames, then set VLAN 10's route targets by hand in an EVPN instance on every leaf.

items.title: EVPN fabric: find the fault
items.summary: The production fabric: jumbo frames on every fabric link (MTU 9216), route target 65000:10010 set by hand on every leaf, BGP EVPN between the leaves' loopbacks, and a server per rack in VLAN 10. Something is off: full-size packets, one direction, one rack, or a path. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: a second segment, with its own route targets
items.summary: A web tier joins on LEAF1 and LEAF3: VLAN 20 (WEB), with WEB1 and WEB3 in it, not carried yet. Give it its own EVPN instance and route target, 65000:10020, so its routes are used only where VLAN 20 is, and full-size packets cross.

items.title: Know it: traceback and DDoS mitigation
Read: how IS-IS works
Learn: IS-IS on a provider backbone
items.summary: Four routers in a square run IS-IS the way provider cores do: one area (49.0001), level 2 only, wide metrics, point-to-point links. PC-A (on R1) reaches PC-B (on R3) over two equal paths. Read what IS-IS shows, then move R1's traffic onto one of them.

items.title: Build it: an IS-IS backbone
items.summary: Four routers in a square, addressed and up, with a loopback each (10.255.0.1-4). Run IS-IS: one area, 49.0001, level 2 only, wide metrics, so PC-A (R1's LAN, 10.1.1.0/24) and PC-B (R3's LAN, 10.3.3.0/24) reach each other over both sides of the square.

items.title: IS-IS: find the fault
items.summary: The backbone should run IS-IS in area 49.0001, level 2 only with wide metrics and point-to-point links, and carry PC-A's and PC-B's LANs over both sides of the square. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: IPv6 in the same IS-IS
items.summary: The backbone needs IPv6 too. IS-IS carries it in the same process: each router advertises its IPv6 prefixes next to its IPv4 ones. Number every link and LAN, run IS-IS for IPv6 on each interface, and PC-A and PC-B reach each other over IPv6 (they autoconfigure their addresses from the LAN prefixes).

items.title: Read: IS-IS areas, the attached bit and route leaking
Learn: IS-IS areas and levels
items.summary: Two areas hang off a level-2 backbone. In area 49.0001, R1 runs level 1 only, dual-homed to R2 and R3 (L1/L2); R4 is the backbone (level 2 only); in area 49.0002, R6 (level 1) sits behind R5 (L1/L2). PC-A and PC-B reach each other, but R1 knows nothing about area 2. See how, then summarize area 2 into the backbone.

items.title: Build it: two areas and a level-2 backbone
items.summary: Six routers are addressed and up, each with a loopback (10.255.0.1-6). Build the IS-IS design: area 49.0001 (R1, R2, R3), the backbone (R4, area 49.0000) and area 49.0002 (R5, R6). R1 and R6 are level 1 only, R4 level 2 only, the others both. PC-A and PC-B must reach each other, through either of area 1's exits.

items.title: IS-IS areas and levels: find the fault
items.summary: Area 49.0001 (R1 level 1, R2 and R3 L1/L2), the backbone R4 (level 2 only) and area 49.0002 (R5 L1/L2, R6 level 1) should carry PC-A to PC-B through either of area 1's exits. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: leak routes into level 1
items.summary: R2's backbone link is now a slow backup circuit (isis metric 100 on both ends). R1 doesn't know: its default points at R2 and R3 alike, since both are one hop away, so half of PC-A's traffic to area 2 takes the slow link. Leak area 2's prefixes into level 1 on R2 and R3, so R1 picks its exit by the whole path.

items.title: Read: stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Learn: stub areas and NSSAs
items.summary: A provider network in three areas. CORE (area 0) has the Internet edge and the server LAN, and gives OSPF a default. The branch, area 1, is a stub area. The factory, area 2, is an NSSA: FAC is the only way to the plant network (172.20.0.0/16) and redistributes it. Read what each area holds, then make area 1 totally stubby.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Build it: a totally stubby area and an NSSA
items.summary: The network runs plain multi-area OSPF: every router knows every route, the plant's included. Shrink what the edges carry. The branch, area 1, needs nothing but a way out: make it totally stubby. The factory, area 2, must keep redistributing the plant network, so it can't be a stub area: make it an NSSA, with a default from ABR2, and the plant route as metric type 1.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Stub areas and NSSAs: find the fault
items.summary: The design: area 1 totally stubby (only a default from ABR1), area 2 an NSSA (FAC redistributes the plant network as type 7, metric type 1; ABR2 translates it for everyone else and gives the area a type 7 default). Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Expand: a virtual link to a stranded area
items.summary: The provider bought a regional network. Its routers sit behind R4: area 5 (R5 and PC5's LAN) hangs off R4, which only joins area 4, and ABR3 joins area 4 to the backbone. Every area must touch area 0. Area 5 doesn't, so it learns nothing from the rest and nobody learns its routes. Rewiring is months away: build a virtual link.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Virtual links: find the fault
items.summary: Area 5 reaches the backbone through a virtual link between ABR3 (router ID 10.255.0.13) and R4 (10.255.4.1) across area 4. PC5 should reach SRV and the Internet. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Expand: OSPFv3 across the areas
items.summary: The routers have IPv6 addresses now: one /64 per link and LAN, a /128 loopback each, area 1's prefixes inside 2001:db8:1::/48 and area 2's inside 2001:db8:2::/48. The PCs autoconfigure. Run OSPFv3 in the same areas. Area 1 is totally stubby for IPv6 too, and ABR2 advertises area 2 as one summary.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: OSPFv3 areas: find the fault
items.summary: OSPFv3 runs in the same areas as IPv4: area 1 totally stubby (ABR1 with no-summary), area 2 summarized as 2001:db8:2::/48 by ABR2. SRV should reach PC1 and PC2 over IPv6. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: OSPF stub areas, NSSAs and virtual links

items.title: Read: scaling iBGP with route reflectors and confederations
Learn: a route reflector instead of a full mesh
items.summary: Three PEs (AS 65000) peer only with RR in the middle, each from its loopback, and each has a customer. RR reflects routes for PE1, its one client so far: PE2 and PE3 are still ordinary iBGP neighbors, so CE2's and CE3's routes don't reach each other. See the reflection rules at work, then finish the job.

items.title: Build it: iBGP through a route reflector
items.summary: The core runs IS-IS (RR in the middle, PE1-PE3 around it, all with loopbacks), and each PE has an eBGP session to its customer. Nothing carries the customers' routes between the PEs yet. Instead of a full mesh, make RR a route reflector with the three PEs as clients.

items.title: Route reflection: find the fault
items.summary: PE1-PE3 (AS 65000) each peer only with RR, from their loopbacks with next-hop-self, and RR reflects for all three. Each PE has a customer. Some customers can't reach others. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: a second route reflector in the same cluster
items.summary: RR is a single point of failure: if it goes, every PE loses every customer route. RR2 now connects to all three PEs (a costlier path while RR is up). Make it a second reflector for the same clients, in the same cluster, so customers keep reaching each other through RR2 when RR fails.

items.title: Expand: a confederation instead of one big mesh
items.summary: Another way to scale iBGP: split the AS. AS 100 becomes confederation 100, made of sub-AS 65001 (R1, R2) and sub-AS 65002 (R3, with a customer LAN). IS-IS runs across all three; X (AS 64500) peers with R1 and must keep seeing one AS, 100. Configure BGP on R1-R3 so PC3 reaches X's network.

items.title: Read: BGP communities, MED and the best-path order
Learn: customers steer their routes with communities
items.summary: A customer (CE1, AS 65101) is dual-homed to the provider (AS 65000): PE1 is its primary link, PE2 its backup. CE1 tags its routes toward PE2 with 65000:80, which the provider's policy turns into local preference 80; it tags its internal network no-export. The provider marks customer routes 65000:100 and sends its peer (PEER, AS 64500) only those. See it work, then swap the customer's primary and backup.

items.title: Build it: a community-driven routing policy
items.summary: The provider (PE1-PE3, AS 65000, iBGP full mesh over IS-IS) connects a dual-homed customer (CE1) and a peer (PEER). Everything is reachable, but nothing is steered: PE2 prefers its own link to the customer, PEER receives the customer's internal network, and PE3 would send PEER anything. Build the policy with communities.

items.title: Communities: find the fault
items.summary: CE1 tags its backup routes (toward PE2) with 65000:80 and its internal network with no-export. PE1 and PE2 turn 65000:80 into local preference 80 and mark every customer route 65000:100; PE3 sends PEER only routes marked 65000:100. Something in the chain is broken. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: protect the customer sessions
items.summary: The customer's contract allows 10 prefixes. A mistake on CE1 could leak many more into the provider, and nothing checks that BGP packets claiming to come from CE1 really do. Protect both customer sessions: close them past 10 prefixes, and accept BGP only from directly connected routers.

items.title: Read: peer groups, dynamic neighbors, timers, dampening and FlowSpec
items.group: BGP peer groups, dynamic neighbors and dampening

items.title: Learn: peer groups and dynamic neighbors
items.summary: A provider core in AS 65000: RR reflects routes for PE1 and PE2, each with a customer behind it. RR has no neighbor statement per PE. Its clients share a peer group, CLIENTS, and RR accepts any PE that connects from inside 10.255.1.0/24, the PE loopbacks. PE3 and its customer are new. Bring PE3 in without touching RR.
items.group: BGP peer groups, dynamic neighbors and dampening

items.title: Build it: a peer group, a listen range, timers and dampening
items.summary: RR has a neighbor statement per PE, three lines each, for PE1 and PE2. PE3 is new and already points at RR, but RR doesn't know it. Replace RR's statements with a peer group and a listen range, so the next PE needs no change on RR. Have RR notice a dead PE within 30 seconds instead of 180, and have PE1 dampen CE1's routes: its lab network (198.51.100.0/24) keeps flapping.
items.group: BGP peer groups, dynamic neighbors and dampening

items.title: Peer groups, listen ranges and dampening: find the fault
items.summary: The design: RR accepts every PE through a listen range over the PE loopbacks (10.255.1.0/24) into peer group CLIENTS, which sets remote-as 65000, update-source, route-reflector-client and a 30-second hold time. PE1 dampens CE1's routes. Every PC reaches every other, and CE1's lab network (198.51.100.1). Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: BGP peer groups, dynamic neighbors and dampening

items.title: Expand: watch a flapping route get suppressed
items.summary: PE1 doesn't dampen yet. With the default 15-minute half-life a suppressed route stays out for most of an hour, too long to watch, so use a 1-minute half-life here: bgp dampening 1 750 2000 4. Then flap CE1's lab network (198.51.100.0/24) and follow the penalty: suppressed at 2000, used again once it decays below 750.
items.group: BGP peer groups, dynamic neighbors and dampening

items.title: Know it: routing policy language and route maps
items.group: Routing policy language and route maps

items.title: Read: MPLS, LDP and the BGP-free core
Learn: labels across a BGP-free core
items.summary: A provider carries two customers across PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2. Only the PEs run BGP: P1 and P2 know the core (IS-IS) and nothing about the customers, yet PC-A reaches PC-B, because the core switches labels with LDP. Follow a packet, then give each P router its own label range.

items.title: Build it: LDP for a BGP-free core
items.summary: The core runs IS-IS, the PEs run BGP, and the customers' routes are in BGP on PE1 and PE2, but PC-A can't reach PC-B: P1 receives plain IP packets for 192.168.2.10 and has no route to it. Run LDP across the core so the PEs label customer traffic and the P routers switch it.

items.title: MPLS: find the fault
items.summary: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 should carry the customers on labels: LDP on every core link, sessions between the loopbacks, P routers without BGP. Customer traffic is failing somewhere in the core. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: hide the core from traceroute
items.summary: Customers' traceroutes show the provider's P routers and their labels. The provider wants them to see only its edge: the PEs. Stop copying the IP TTL into the labels where traffic enters the core.

items.title: Expand: ping the path, then make the IGP wait for it
items.summary: The core has two paths from PE1 to PE2: the short one through P1 and P2, and a long one through P3 (metric 100 per link). LDP runs everywhere and the customers reach each other. Follow the labels with an LSP ping, break one LDP session while its link stays up, watch IP routing stay happy while labeled traffic dies, then let LDP-IGP synchronization route around the gap.

items.title: Expand: a core that routes around missing labels
items.summary: LDP runs on every link and the customers reach each other over the short path. Nothing yet tells IS-IS to avoid a link whose labels are missing: if the P1-P2 LDP session failed, IS-IS would keep sending traffic that way, unlabeled, into a P router that drops it. Configure LDP-IGP synchronization and session protection on the five core routers. Check tests your network with the P1-P2 session broken on a copy.

items.title: MPLS operations: find the fault
items.summary: The five core routers run LDP with synchronization and session protection, and the customers' traffic takes the short path through P1 and P2. A ticket says something changed. Use the LSP tools and the sync and neighbor shows to find the port, the session or the setting at fault. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: LDP passwords and label filtering
items.summary: An LDP session is a TCP session anyone on a core link could try to open, and every router advertises a label for every prefix it knows, link addresses included. Authenticate every session with TCP MD5, refuse sessions without a password, and advertise labels for the loopbacks only, which is all the BGP next hops need.

items.title: Read: MPLS Layer 3 VPNs on the PE
Learn: two customers, one core
items.summary: A provider carries two customers across PE1 - P1 - PE2. Both use 192.168.1.0/24 at their first site and 192.168.2.0/24 at their second; each is a VRF on the PEs, with its own route distinguisher and route target. Customer A works. Customer B's second site was connected today, and its VRF on PE2 isn't finished.

items.title: Build it: a customer's L3VPN
items.summary: The core is ready: IS-IS, LDP, and iBGP between PE1's and PE2's loopbacks. Customer A's CEs are configured and wait for the provider: CE-A1 (AS 65001) peers with 172.16.1.1, CE-A2 (AS 65002) with 172.16.2.1. Give customer A a VRF on both PEs, carry its routes between them in VPNv4, and connect its sites.

items.title: L3VPN: find the fault
items.summary: PE1 - P1 - PE2 carries customers A and B, both with sites behind both PEs and the same addresses, in VRF A (65000:1) and VRF B (65000:2). One customer, or both, can't reach its other site. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: shared services
items.summary: The provider runs a server for its customers (SRV, 10.100.0.10) in its own VRF on PE2, SVC (rd 65000:100), which exports route target 65000:100. Customer A has signed up for it. Give customer A's sites the server's route, and the server routes back to customer A, without merging the two VRFs.

items.title: Expand: Internet access through an Internet VRF
items.summary: Customer A's sites use public addresses, 203.0.113.0/25 and 203.0.113.128/25, and now buy Internet access. The provider's Internet VRF on PE2, INET (rd 65000:999), peers with an upstream that sends it a default route, and exports its routes with route target 65000:999. Give customer A the default route, and the Internet the way back to customer A.

items.title: Expand: one AS at every site
items.summary: Customer A uses AS 65001 at both sites. Each CE receives the other site's LAN with AS path 65000 65001, finds its own AS in it and drops the route as a loop: the VPN carries the routes, but the sites can't reach each other. Fix it on the provider's side.

items.title: Expand: unified MPLS, one LSP across three IGP domains
items.summary: Two access areas (IS-IS level 1) hang off a level-2 core. The ABRs summarize their area's loopbacks into the core and leak nothing back, so PE1 knows PE2 only through its default route, and LDP has no label for a default: the customer's L3VPN is down. Carry the PE loopbacks in BGP with labels instead: each PE sends its loopback to its ABR, the ABRs reflect them to each other and down to the other PE as the next hop (next-hop-self all), and every router pushes the label it was given under the transport label toward the next hop. The core never learns a PE loopback.
items.group: Unified MPLS: labeled BGP between IGP domains

items.title: Unified MPLS: find the fault
items.summary: The three domains carry the customer over one label-switched path: the PE loopbacks travel in BGP with labels, the ABRs reflecting them as next hop. A ticket says the sites can't reach each other. Follow the labels (show ip bgp labels, show mpls forwarding-table) from PE to ABR to ABR to PE, find the router whose label is missing or wrong, fix it, and press Check. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: Unified MPLS: labeled BGP between IGP domains

items.title: Read: Layer 2 VPNs and Carrier Ethernet
Learn: one customer's LAN stretched across the provider
items.summary: The provider's core (PE1 - P1 - PE2) runs IS-IS and LDP, with each router's loopback as its LDP ID. Customer A wants its two routers on one LAN: CE-A1 and CE-A2 share 192.168.12.0/24 and run OSPF, but today they're on two separate cables into two PEs. Customer B tags its traffic VLAN 200 at one site and VLAN 300 at the other. Build an Ethernet over MPLS pseudowire for each: the whole port for A, one VLAN (rewritten) for B.

items.title: Build it: two E-Lines across the core
items.summary: The core is up (IS-IS, LDP, loopbacks 10.255.0.1 on PE1 and 10.255.0.2 on PE2). The orders: customer A gets a port-based E-Line between PE1 Gi0/0 and PE2 Gi0/0, VC ID 100, so its routers become OSPF neighbors. Customer B gets a VLAN-based E-Line, VC ID 200, between VLAN 200 on PE1 Gi0/1 and VLAN 300 on PE2 Gi0/1, as service instances 200 and 300 that pop the customer's tag.

items.title: L2VPN: find the fault
items.summary: Both E-Lines worked: customer A's routers were OSPF neighbors across the provider, and customer B's VLAN 200 site reached its VLAN 300 site. Then a change broke one or both. A pseudowire is down for a reason show mpls l2transport vc detail names (signaling, VC ID, MTU, the circuit), or it's up and the frames still don't arrive (the label path, the flow points' tags).

items.title: Expand: one LAN for three sites (VPLS)
items.summary: Customer C has three sites, on PE1, PE2 and PE3, and wants them on one LAN (an E-LAN): 10.30.0.0/24, OSPF between all three CEs. Point-to-point pseudowires can't do it: build a VPLS instance on each PE, a VFI with a full mesh of pseudowires to the other two, joined to the customer's untagged flow point in a bridge domain. Frames that arrive over one pseudowire never leave over another (split horizon), which is why the mesh must be full.

items.title: Expand: customer VLANs through a metro network (802.1ad)
items.summary: A metro Ethernet provider (MSW1 and MSW2, a trunk between them) carries two customers. Customer D has VLANs 10 and 20 at both sites, trunked into the provider; customer E's PCs are untagged, and numbered in the same 10.10.0.0/24 as D's VLAN 10. Give each customer one provider VLAN (an S-VLAN: 100 for D, 200 for E) with 802.1ad: a dot1q-tunnel port puts every frame, with its own tag, inside the provider's VLAN, so D's two VLANs cross as one and the customers never meet.

items.title: Expand: watching the E-Line with Ethernet OAM (CFM)
items.summary: Customer B's E-Line now joins two switches (VLAN 200 at site 1, VLAN 300 at site 2), and both the provider and the customer want to know the moment it breaks, and where. 802.1ag CFM: the provider monitors its EVC from flow point to flow point with up MEPs at level 4, across the pseudowire; the customer monitors its own end to end with down MEPs at level 6 on its uplinks. A higher level passes through a lower one's MEPs, so the customer's checks cross the provider untouched; the provider's MIPs at level 6 let the customer's linktrace see the provider's edges.

items.title: Ethernet OAM: find the fault
items.summary: The provider's level-4 MEPs and the customer's level-6 MEPs all heard each other, until a change. Now a MEP lists no remote, or show ethernet cfm errors reports a cross-connect or an error CCM. The data may still flow: CFM faults are often in CFM itself. Read the remote MEP tables, the errors and the local MEPs, and find the one change.

items.title: Expand: a ring that heals in 50 ms (G.8032)
items.summary: A metro access ring: AGG1 - AGG2 - ACC2 - ACC1 and back to AGG1, each router bridging VLAN 100 between its two ring ports and its customer port (flow points in bridge-domain 100). Bridge domains run no spanning tree, so the ring is a loop and a broadcast storm has taken the whole service down. G.8032 Ethernet ring protection breaks the loop at one link, the ring protection link (RPL) between ACC1 and ACC2, and moves the break to any link that fails, in tens of milliseconds.

items.title: G.8032: find the fault
items.summary: The ring METRO worked: ACC2 owned the RPL toward ACC1, every node was Idle, and cutting any link healed within a second. Then a change. Now part of the ring can't reach SRV, or a failure no longer heals. G.8032's state is in show ethernet ring g8032 status and brief on each node: the role, the state, which port is blocked and whether R-APS arrives on both.

items.title: Expand: a hub and its branches (E-Tree)
items.summary: Customer F wants an E-Tree: the hub (HUB, behind PE1) is the root, and the branches are leaves. BR1 and BR2 sit on PE2, BR3 on PE3. Every leaf reaches the root, and no leaf reaches another, on the same PE or not. Build it from VPLS: the root's PE has a pseudowire to each leaf PE, the leaf PEs have one to the root's PE only, and VPLS split horizon at PE1 stops it relaying between them. On PE2, the two leaves share a split-horizon group.

items.title: Expand: a customer through another operator (E-Access)
items.summary: Customer G's site 1 isn't on your network: an access provider's switch (ASW1) reaches it and hands its traffic to you at an external network-to-network interface (ENNI), PE1 Gi0/3, inside S-VLAN 300. That's E-Access: the access provider's service ends at the ENNI. Configure its side (802.1ad: the customer's port into S-VLAN 300, a trunk to you) and yours: a flow point on the ENNI for S-VLAN 300 that pops the S-tag, and a pseudowire to PE2, where site 2 is on your own UNI. The customer's VLAN 10 crosses untouched.

items.title: Read: segment routing over MPLS
Learn: labels from the IGP
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is running; there's no LDP anywhere. Follow the labels, then give a new service address its own SID.

items.title: Build it: segment routing on a BGP-free core
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. IS-IS and BGP are up, but nothing is labeled yet: PE1 sends PC-B's traffic as plain IP, and P1 drops it.

items.title: Segment routing: find the fault
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is built, but customers are complaining, or will the next time a link fails. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: migrate from LDP, with a mapping server
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. The core ran LDP; segment routing has been turned on everywhere except PE2, whose software can't run it. Move PE1's traffic to SR labels anyway.

items.title: Read: TI-LFA, SR-TE and the PCE
Learn: TI-LFA repairs
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is running everywhere. TI-LFA is on everywhere but P1. Read the repairs, then close P1's gap.

items.title: Build it: TI-LFA everywhere, and a low-delay policy
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is running everywhere. Site B bought a low-delay service: PE1 must send its traffic along the bottom (a shorter fiber route), though IS-IS prefers the top. And the whole core should survive a link failure without a blip.

items.title: TI-LFA and SR-TE: find the fault
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is running everywhere. TI-LFA runs everywhere, and PE1 steers site B's traffic (color 100) along the bottom with policy LOW-DELAY. Something is off: the low-delay service, or the protection. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: low delay on the way back
items.summary: A provider carries two sites across a ring of six routers: PE1 - P1 - P2 - PE2 on top, PE1 - P3 - P4 - PE2 below. IS-IS runs the core (level 2, wide metrics); the bottom links cost 20, the top ones 10, so traffic takes the top. Only the PEs run BGP, so P1 to P4 know nothing about the customers: they carry customer traffic only on labels. Each router's SID index is its loopback's last byte: PE1 1, PE2 2, P1 11, P2 12, P3 13, P4 14. Segment routing is running everywhere. PE1 steers site B's traffic along the bottom with policy LOW-DELAY. Policies are one-way: PC-B's replies still take the top. Steer them too.

items.title: Read: SRv6 and flexible algorithm
Know it: segment routing control planes: IS-IS, OSPF and BGP
items.group: SR control planes: IS-IS, OSPF and BGP

items.title: Know it: traffic engineering with RSVP-TE
Learn: a tunnel that takes the long way round
items.summary: Five routers under IS-IS level 2: the short path from R1 to R4 runs through R2 (metric 20), the long one through R3 and R5 (30). Every link has mpls traffic-eng tunnels and 500000 kbps reservable, and R1 already heads Tunnel1 to R4 along an explicit path over R3 and R5, reserving 200000 kbps, with autoroute announce. Read what RSVP signaled, follow the labels, then let CSPF choose the path instead and watch the tunnel move to R2.

items.title: Build: steer traffic onto the long path with RSVP-TE
items.summary: The TE topology is ready: mpls traffic-eng tunnels everywhere, 500000 kbps reservable per link, IS-IS carrying the TE extensions. The short path through R2 is for other customers; this one's traffic must take R3 and R5 both ways, with 200000 kbps reserved. Build an explicit path and a tunnel on R1, the mirror image on R4, and let autoroute announce send the traffic in.

items.title: RSVP-TE: find the fault
items.summary: Both tunnels run the long way round, R1 to R4 over R3 and R5 and back, each reserving 200000 kbps, with a dynamic path option as fallback. A ticket says the traffic has moved, or stopped. Read the tunnel's status and the reasons each path option failed, check the links' TE and RSVP settings, fix the cause and press Check. A reset picks a new fault.

items.title: Expand: when the short path is full, CSPF takes the long one
items.summary: R1's Tunnel1 to R4 is dynamic now: it sits on the short path over R2, reserving 300000 of the 500000 kbps each link offers, and autoroute announce sends all traffic for R4 into it. A second service needs its own 300000 kbps tunnel to R4. There isn't room on the short path, so a dynamic Tunnel2 will have to go the long way round: CSPF only considers links with enough bandwidth left. Steer the customer's prefix into it with a static route.

items.title: Know it: VPN services beyond one provider: inter-AS, CSC and mVPN
items.group: VPN services: inter-AS, CSC and mVPN

items.title: Read: fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF, NSR and BGP PIC
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Learn: how long a failure lasts
items.summary: R1 and R2 run OSPF across a switch, SW1, with a slower path through R3 for when SW1's path fails. That backup works, but how fast? When R2's port behind SW1 fails, R1's own port stays up: R1 only notices when R2's hellos stop for the dead interval (40 s), then waits 5 s more before SPF. Bring that down: BFD between R1 and R2, and SPF in milliseconds.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Build it: subsecond OSPF convergence
items.summary: The same network, with BFD this time on R1 only, and nothing else tuned. The requirement: whatever fails between R1 and R2 (either port behind SW1, or SW1 itself), PC1 and PC2 are back within a second, over R3. BFD must detect within 150 ms.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Fast convergence: find the fault
items.summary: The design: BFD between R1 and R2 on g0/1 for OSPF (50 ms, multiplier 3: 150 ms), timers throttle spf 50 200 5000 and carrier-delay msec 0 on both, so any failure between them costs PC1 and PC2 under a second. Something is off: traffic still fails over, just too slowly. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Expand: a switchover with no loss (SSO and NSF)
items.summary: Each PC hangs off one router, so if R1 or R2 restarts there is no way around it. Both routers have a standby route processor. Make a route processor failure invisible: stateful switchover keeps the forwarding table in place, and graceful restart (NSF) keeps OSPF's neighbors from tearing down the adjacency while the new active processor catches up.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Expand: BGP PIC with add-path
items.summary: A provider core (AS 65000): IS-IS and LDP, a P router that runs no BGP, and a route reflector beside it. The customer, CE (AS 65101), is dual-homed to PE1 and PE2; PC3 is behind PE3. The core already reacts in milliseconds (carrier-delay 0, fast SPF), but when PE1 fails PC3 still loses the customer for over 5 s: the reflector sent PE3 only its best path, through PE1. Give PE3 the second path in advance and have it install that as a backup.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: BGP PIC and add-path: find the fault
items.summary: The design: RR sends PE3 two paths to the customer (bgp additional-paths send, select best 2, neighbor 10.255.0.3 advertise additional-paths best 2); PE3 receives them and installs the second as a backup (bgp additional-paths receive, install). PE1's failure should cost PC3 under a second. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: Fast convergence: BFD, timers, NSF and BGP PIC

items.title: Read: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, 6PE, NAT64 and MAP-T
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Learn: IPv6 in an IPv4 tunnel
items.summary: Two IPv6-only sites, PC1 behind R1 and PC2 behind R2. Their provider (ISP) carries IPv4 only. A manual tunnel joins them: R1 and R2 each have a Tunnel0 that wraps IPv6 packets in IPv4 (IP protocol 41) between their outside addresses. R1 routes PC2's LAN into the tunnel; R2 has no route back yet.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Build it: an IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel with OSPFv3
items.summary: The two IPv6 sites can't reach each other: the provider between them runs IPv4 only. Build a manual tunnel between R1 (198.51.100.2) and R2 (203.0.113.2), addressed 2001:db8:ffff::/64, and run OSPFv3 across it, so each site learns the other's LAN.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: IPv6 tunnels: find the fault
items.summary: The design: a manual IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel (tunnel mode ipv6ip) between R1 (198.51.100.2) and R2 (203.0.113.2), addressed 2001:db8:ffff::/64, with OSPFv3 over it. PC1 and PC2 should reach each other. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Expand: 6to4, a tunnel with no destination
items.summary: A manual tunnel needs both ends configured for every pair of sites. 6to4 needs none: each site's prefix is 2002:<its outside IPv4 address in hex>::/48, so the IPv4 address to send to is inside every destination. R1's outside address 198.51.100.2 is c633:6402, so its site is 2002:c633:6402::/48 (its LAN 2002:c633:6402:1::/64); R2's 203.0.113.2 gives 2002:cb00:7102::/48.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Expand: NAT64 to an IPv4-only server
items.summary: Site 1 is IPv6-only, and SRV (192.0.2.10, at the provider) is IPv4-only. Make R1 a stateful NAT64 gateway: IPv6 hosts reach any IPv4 host at 64:ff9b:: plus its IPv4 address, so SRV is 64:ff9b::192.0.2.10 (64:ff9b::c000:20a). R1 gives translated traffic an address from 198.51.100.64/27, which the ISP already routes to R1.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: NAT64: find the fault
items.summary: R1 is a stateful NAT64 gateway: nat64 enable on g0/1 and g0/0, prefix 64:ff9b::/96, pool SITE1 (198.51.100.65-94) for the sources that NAT64-SOURCES permits (2001:db8:1::/64), with overload; the ISP routes 198.51.100.64/27 to R1. PC1 should reach SRV at 64:ff9b::c000:20a. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Expand: 6PE across an MPLS core
items.summary: A provider core in AS 65000: PE1, P and PE2 run IS-IS and LDP, IPv4 only. The PEs peer in iBGP between their loopbacks. Each PE has an IPv6 site. P must stay IPv6-free: carry IPv6 between the sites with 6PE, so the PEs exchange IPv6 prefixes in BGP, labeled, and P only switches labels.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: 6PE: find the fault
items.summary: 6PE across an IPv4 MPLS core: PE1 and PE2 (iBGP between loopbacks 10.255.0.1 and .2) exchange their IPv6 LANs in BGP's IPv6 family, activated and with send-label on both; P runs IS-IS and LDP only. PC1 and PC2 should reach each other. Something is off. A reset picks a new fault.
items.group: IPv6 across IPv4: tunnels, NAT64 and 6PE

items.title: Read: multicast and PIM sparse mode
Learn: the shared tree and the shortest path
items.summary: A provider carries a news channel, 239.1.1.1, from a headend (SRC, behind R1) to two customer sites (RCV-A behind R3, RCV-B behind R4). The core is a square, R1-R2-R4 on top and R1-R3 below, with a slow backup link from R3 to R4 (OSPF cost 100). OSPF carries everything. The receivers are routers that joined the group on their LAN interface (ip igmp join-group), so they answer pings to it. R2 is the RP (10.255.0.2). PIM sparse mode is running. Follow the stream, see the trees in show ip mroute, then keep one site on the shared tree.

items.title: Build it: PIM sparse mode with a static RP
items.summary: A provider carries a news channel, 239.1.1.1, from a headend (SRC, behind R1) to two customer sites (RCV-A behind R3, RCV-B behind R4). The core is a square, R1-R2-R4 on top and R1-R3 below, with a slow backup link from R3 to R4 (OSPF cost 100). OSPF carries everything. The receivers are routers that joined the group on their LAN interface (ip igmp join-group), so they answer pings to it. R2 is the RP (10.255.0.2). Unicast works, and the receivers have joined; the routers don't route multicast yet.

items.title: Multicast: find the fault
items.summary: A provider carries a news channel, 239.1.1.1, from a headend (SRC, behind R1) to two customer sites (RCV-A behind R3, RCV-B behind R4). The core is a square, R1-R2-R4 on top and R1-R3 below, with a slow backup link from R3 to R4 (OSPF cost 100). OSPF carries everything. The receivers are routers that joined the group on their LAN interface (ip igmp join-group), so they answer pings to it. R2 is the RP (10.255.0.2). items.title: Expand: the provider's edge, policing to contract
items.summary: PE1 takes two customers into a 10 Mb/s core link to PE2 and the data center (DC, 10.30.0.10). Each customer bought 1 Mb/s of real-time traffic (EF) and 4 Mb/s of business data. CUST-A sends 512 kb/s of calls (EF) and 9 Mb/s of data; CUST-B marks all of its 8 Mb/s EF. With nothing configured, the core link is one FIFO queue and A's calls lose like everything else. Police each customer as it arrives (REALTIME to 1 Mb/s, the excess dropped; data within 4 Mb/s re-marked af11, beyond it af12), then queue the core: REALTIME priority, BUSINESS a guarantee with WRED, so out-of-contract af12 is dropped before af11.

items.title: Know it: model-driven telemetry with gRPC and gNMI
Learn: a router streams to a collector (dial-out)
items.summary: COLL runs Telegraf, listening for telemetry on TCP 57500. Instead of an SNMP manager polling R1 every few minutes, R1 will push: its CPU every 10 seconds, and its interfaces' state the moment it changes. Each is a configured subscription: what to send (a YANG path, by the module's prefix), how (yang-push, kvGPB), when (periodic, or on change) and where (the receiver).

items.title: Build it: gNMI and telemetry over mutual TLS
items.summary: Plain gRPC crosses the network readable, and anyone can connect. Secure both directions with certificates from the lab CA (COLL has ca.crt, its own and a client certificate). Dial-in: R1 runs the TLS gNMI server with its own certificate and accepts only clients with a certificate the lab CA signed, and COLL reads it with gnmic. Dial-out: R2 streams its memory to Telegraf's mutual-TLS listener (57502), proving itself with its own certificate.

items.title: Telemetry: find the fault
items.summary: R1 streamed its CPU and interface state to COLL, R2 its memory over mutual TLS, and COLL read R1 over gNMI. Then a change. Now something no longer arrives, or gnmic is turned away. The router says why a subscription is invalid or disconnected; gnmic says why it fails.

items.title: Expand: a BGP session watched on change
items.summary: R1 and R2 now run eBGP. A session that drops and comes back within a minute never shows in a 60-second poll; on change, the router sends the moment it happens. Watch R1's BGP neighbors on change, sourced from R1's loopback (an address that doesn't depend on one interface, the one a collector's firewall rules would name), and read the same state over gNMI.

items.title: Hub and spoke: find the fault

If either P router fails, traffic takes the other, still labeled. Every address is configured and the customers are waiting; the provider's routing is yours.

items.title: Capstone: dual-ISP Internet edge with BGP
items.summary: Connect an online shop to two providers with BGP: eBGP from each edge, the company's /24 anchored by Null0, iBGP between the edges, local preference to leave through the primary, prepending so the Internet comes in through it too, and defaults into OSPF with metrics so the campus follows. The campus and providers are in service; both edges are blank.

items.title: Capstone: dual-ISP Internet edge with BGP, Operate
items.summary: Halden Outdoor's edge from the build is in service, built to the same brief: both edges peer with their provider and with each other, ISP-A is preferred both ways (local preference 200 out, prepending toward ISP-B in), and the campus follows EDGE-A's default. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: segmented campus with VRF-Lite
items.summary: Separate a clinic's staff, guests and building systems on one set of switches: a VRF per segment on both distribution switches with HSRP gateways, a transit VLAN per VRF to its own firewall interface, and a firewall that lets each segment out (with PAT) and pins the camera to its vendor's cloud. Everything is cabled and the hosts are addressed; the switches and the firewall are blank.

items.title: Capstone: segmented campus with VRF-Lite, Operate
items.summary: Mossgiel Clinic's segmented campus from the build is in service, built to the same brief: VRFs CORP, GUEST and IOT on both distribution switches with HSRP, one transit VLAN and firewall interface per segment, PAT for all, and the camera pinned to its cloud. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: pharmacy WAN failover over MPLS, GRE over IPsec and LTE
items.summary: Give a pharmacy branch three ways out: MPLS for the prescription system, broadband for browsing and an IPsec-protected GRE tunnel to head office, and LTE behind the carrier's NAT. IP SLA probes, pinned to the links they watch, move the routes when a provider fails with the ports still up. The provider, head office and Internet are in service; the branch router is blank.

items.title: Capstone: pharmacy WAN failover over MPLS, GRE over IPsec and LTE, Operate
items.summary: Brightwater's branch from the build is in service, built to the same brief: MPLS for RX, broadband for browsing and the protected tunnel, LTE as the last resort, and probes that move the routes. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: hybrid cloud over two IPsec tunnels with BGP
items.summary: Connect a campus to an application in a cloud network the way cloud VPN services expect: two route-based IPsec tunnels, eBGP over each, the campus aggregate anchored by Null0, both tunnels in use, and the cloud's prefix into OSPF so cloud traffic avoids the firewall's NAT. Campus, firewall, provider and cloud are in service; the VPN router is blank.

items.title: Capstone: hybrid cloud over two IPsec tunnels with BGP, Operate
items.summary: Northwind's cloud connection from the build is in service, built to the same brief: two IPsec tunnels, BGP over both, both in use, and the cloud's route in OSPF. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: remote site over LEO satellite and LTE
items.summary: Bring a clinic with no fiber online: satellite and LTE by DHCP, both behind the carriers' NAT, local breakout with PAT per link, DMVPN spoke tunnels the site itself opens (IPsec through NAT), OSPF to head office, and an IP SLA probe that moves everything to LTE when the satellite fails. Carriers, Internet and head office are in service; the site router is blank.
items.topic: Capstone: remote site over satellite and LTE

items.title: Capstone: remote site over LEO satellite and LTE, Operate
items.summary: Ridgeline's clinic from the build is in service, built to the same brief: satellite first, LTE as backup, tunnels the site opens, and a probe that moves everything. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.
items.topic: Capstone: remote site over satellite and LTE

items.title: Capstone: remote-access VPN to an internal application
items.summary: Give field adjusters working from home and from hotels the claims ticketing system at head office, and nothing else: the firewall becomes a VPN headend (an address pool, per-user sign-in, a group policy that splits and filters the tunnel, a tunnel group picked by name), and the campus routes the pool back. Home, hotel, Internet and head office's campus are in service; the headend and the route back are yours. The firewall's commands are ASA-style; NetDrill's VPN client on the PCs stands in for the vendor's.

items.title: Capstone: remote-access VPN to an internal application, Operate
items.summary: Larkspur's VPN from the build is in service, built to the same brief: kim and sam connect to 203.0.113.2 as group FIELD, get addresses from 10.99.0.10-10.99.0.250, tunnel only 10.20.0.0/16, and reach TICKETS on HTTPS only; CORE routes the pool back. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: SD-WAN migration (design)
items.summary: A design capstone. Study a retailer's running WAN (MPLS with an idle IPsec backup, SaaS backhauled to HQ), then design its SD-WAN replacement: transports, controllers, application-aware routing, segments, Internet breakout and a cutover that never strands a store. NetDrill doesn't simulate SD-WAN controllers: the target is drawn, and the questions and your written plan are graded. ENCOR 1.2 asks you to explain these elements.

items.title: Capstone: a regional ISP core
items.summary: Turn up a regional ISP's new core: IS-IS between six provider routers, LDP so the P routers carry customer traffic without BGP, a route reflector beside the core for three PEs, a dual-homed customer steered with communities, and limits on the customer sessions. The customers, the transit provider and every address are in service; the provider's routing is yours.

items.title: Capstone: a regional ISP core, Operate
items.summary: Northwind's core from the build is in service, built to the same brief: IS-IS level 2 with wide metrics, LDP everywhere, P routers without BGP, the PEs reflected by RR, CUST-B's backup tag turned into local preference 80, customer routes tagged 65000:100, and maximum-prefix 10 on customer sessions. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: an ISP's TV and business core
items.summary: Move a regional ISP's core to segment routing and launch TV on it: SR on five provider routers so the core stays BGP-free, TI-LFA so a link failure costs milliseconds, an SSM channel from a headend in the data center to set-top boxes in two towns, and an SR-TE policy that keeps a business customer off the TV path. IS-IS, BGP and every address are in service.

items.title: Capstone: an ISP's TV and business core, Operate
items.summary: Riverbend's core from the build is in service, built to the same brief: segment routing and TI-LFA on all five provider routers, the TV channel by SSM from the headend, and site A's traffic to site B steered through P2 by policy BUSINESS. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: Capstone: dual-stack POPs in OSPF areas
items.summary: Grow a regional ISP from one flat core into POPs: an OSPF area per POP behind an aggregation router (links summarized, loopbacks never), LDP across the areas so the core stays BGP-free, a route reflector that serves three PEs through one peer group, 6PE so a dual-stack customer and the data center exchange IPv6 across an IPv4-only core, then BFD everywhere, BGP PIC at the data center PE, NSF on the P routers and dampening at the customer edge. The customer, the data center and every address are in service; the provider's routing is yours.

items.title: Capstone: dual-stack POPs in OSPF areas, Operate
items.summary: Harbor Line's POPs from the build are in service, built to the same brief: an OSPF area per POP with the links summarized and the loopbacks exact, LDP everywhere, RR serving the PEs through peer group CLIENTS, 6PE for the dual-stack customer and the data center, BFD and fast SPF, BGP PIC at PE3, NSF on the P routers and dampening on PE1 and PE2. A ticket has just come in. Reset brings the next one.

items.title: VLANs and inter-VLAN routing reps
items.summary: a new campus every rep: router-on-a-stick, two switches on a trunk, or a layer-3 switch; the VLAN numbers, names, subnets, ports, trunk rules and the server's place change

items.title: Spanning tree and EtherChannel reps
items.summary: a new plan every rep: the root (and backup root) of each VLAN, Rapid PVST+ or not, how each doubled link is bundled and with which modes, PortFast and BPDU Guard, new VLANs and subnets

items.title: Static routing reps
items.summary: a new set of sites every rep: the shape, the addresses, who gets by with a default route, a summary for a site with two networks, a floating backup and a host route change

items.title: OSPF reps
items.summary: a new network every rep: the shape, the addresses and the requirements change

items.title: HSRP and VRRP reps
items.summary: a new gateway pair every rep: HSRP or VRRP, the group, which router leads and at what priority, the tracking decrement, version 2, and sometimes a second group that shares the load

items.title: ACLs reps
items.summary: a new policy every rep: which laptop is the contractor's and how it is kept from the servers, what guests may reach on the web server, a Telnet ban, new addresses and list names

items.title: DHCP reps
items.summary: a new site every rep: the subnets, which router serves and which relays, the excluded range, the DNS server and domain, and sometimes a third LAN the server has no route back to

items.title: NAT reps
items.summary: a new edge every rep: the private LAN, the public addresses, PAT on the interface or a pool, a numbered or named inside list, the published server and a forwarded port

items.title: Device access (SSH) reps
items.summary: a new device to lock down every rep: where it sits, the accounts, the key, the lines and who may connect change

items.title: Multi-area OSPF reps
items.summary: a new plan every rep: the area numbers and addresses, router IDs, a stub or totally stubby area, an NSSA with a redistributed network, a summary or a filter at the border, and a third area that needs a virtual link

items.title: EIGRP reps
items.summary: a new EIGRP network every rep: the shape, the addresses, the AS and the requirements (authentication, stubs, delay, variance) change

items.title: BGP reps
items.summary: a new company and provider every rep: one edge router, OSPF inside with BGP at the edge, iBGP between two routers, two providers (the shorter AS path, or a policy out or both ways), or two sites in one AS; the AS numbers, blocks, addresses and a session password change

items.title: Redistribution reps
items.summary: a new boundary every rep: one boundary router (either side EIGRP, the other OSPF; E1 externals; a lab network kept out by a route map) or two (tags both ways, a distribute list or a distance against OSPF's copies, a summary into OSPF); the addresses, AS, process and tags change
items.group: Route control: redistribution, tags, distance and PBR

items.title: VRF-lite reps
items.summary: a new pair of routers every rep: two or three customers with the same addresses, their names, VLANs and link addresses, one customer sometimes on already in the global table, and each customer's routing (static, OSPF, EIGRP or eBGP inside its VRF)

items.title: IS-IS reps
items.summary: a new IS-IS network every rep: the shape, the addresses, the area and system IDs, the levels and the requirements change

items.title: Route reflectors and confederations reps
items.summary: a new provider core every rep: a route reflector with three PEs and their customers (sometimes a second reflector in the same cluster), or a confederation of two sub-ASes; the AS numbers, loopbacks, links and customer addresses change

items.title: MPLS and LDP reps
items.summary: a new BGP-free core every rep: two or three P routers, IS-IS or OSPF underneath, new loopbacks, link and customer addresses and AS numbers; sometimes a label range per P router, sometimes a core hidden from the customers' traceroutes

items.title: Segment routing reps
items.summary: a new ring every rep: the loopback scheme, SID plan and SRGB, the bottom links' metric, addresses and AS; sometimes a service loopback that needs its own SID, TI-LFA everywhere, or a low-delay SR-TE policy along the bottom

items.title: Multicast reps
items.summary: a new channel every rep: the group, addresses and backup cost, which router is the RP and how the others learn it (static, Auto-RP or BSR), sometimes a source-specific second channel or a site kept on the shared tree
